questions.q: What problem does VAR/RETURN solve in a formula that repeats the same subexpression twice?
options: It calculates the subexpression once and reuses the result, instead of computing it twice
It automatically creates a new relationship
It removes the need for CALCULATE entirely
It converts the measure into a calculated column
questions.explain: VAR names a computed value once; RETURN can reference that name as many times as needed without recomputing it — improving both performance and readability.

questions.q: Besides performance, what's another benefit of using named variables in DAX?
options: Readability and easier debugging — you can temporarily return just a variable to check its value
Variables are required before a formula can be saved
Variables convert row context into filter context automatically
Variables automatically fix syntax errors
questions.explain: A well-named variable documents what a subexpression represents, and swapping RETURN to output just one variable is a fast way to isolate what's producing an unexpected result.

questions.q: What does DIVIDE do differently from the plain / operator?
options: It performs multiplication instead of division
It returns blank (or a specified alternate value) instead of an error when the denominator is zero or blank
It always rounds the result to the nearest whole number
It only works inside calculated columns, not measures
questions.explain: Plain division throws an error on a zero or blank denominator. DIVIDE handles that gracefully, which is why it's the recommended default for division in DAX.

questions.q: Why is DIVIDE recommended as the default over / for report-facing formulas?
options: Because / only works with whole numbers
Because / is deprecated and no longer works in DAX
Because DIVIDE is required syntax for every measure
Because a zero denominator with / produces a jarring error in the visual, while DIVIDE returns a clean blank instead
questions.explain: In a report someone else is using, an unhandled division error is a poor experience — DIVIDE avoids that by design.

questions.q: Which of these is part of the closing best-practices checklist from this lesson?
options: Never use variables in a measure
Avoid CALCULATE whenever possible
Fully qualify column references, even within the same table
Always prefer calculated columns over measures
questions.explain: The checklist recommends clear measure names, variables for repeated subexpressions, DIVIDE over /, fully qualified columns, and simple filter arguments where possible.
